record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.context_brief: Regime dependence of hot wind phases
record.original_question: Why do the two nearby O9-type dwarf stars 10 Lac and μ Col require different wind diagnostics, and how regime-dependent is the presence of a hot wind component in weak-wind stars? The problem includes determining whether the hot phase is sometimes only the tail of a wind-structure distribution, whether it can become the dominant wind component in stars subject to the weak-wind problem, and whether the transition between these regimes is smooth.

evidence.quote: Recently, this idea got new support from JWST mid-IR observations of the nearby O9 dwarf 10 Lac, where forbidden high-ionization fine-structure emission lines indicate a ten-times higher Ṁ (Law et al. 2024). Notably, these lines are not visible in the JWST mid-IR spectrum of μ Col, raising the question why two stars with very similar spectral types require so different diagnostics.

Nonetheless, more observational guidance would be extremely helpful as it is so far unclear how regime-dependent the presence of a hotter wind component is and whether there is a smooth transition from the hot phase actually being a tail of a distribution to presumably becoming a dominant component in stars subjected to the “weak-wind problem”.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider radiation-driven stellar winds from hot massive stars of late-O spectral type, in particular two nearby O9-type dwarf stars: 10 Lac and μ Col. Empirical mass-loss rates Ṁ derived from cool-wind UV/optical diagnostics in such stars are often found to be far below predictions of standard line-driven wind theory; this discrepancy is known as the weak-wind problem. A proposed resolution is that a substantial fraction of the wind exists in a hot, X-ray/EUV-emitting phase that is invisible to traditional cool-wind diagnostics but accessible through forbidden high-ionization fine-structure mid-infrared emission lines (for example [Ne II], [Ne III], [S IV]).

Observations show that 10 Lac exhibits such forbidden high-ionization fine-structure mid-IR emission lines implying a mass-loss rate roughly an order of magnitude larger than that inferred from UV diagnostics, while μ Col, despite a very similar spectral type, does not show these mid-IR lines.

Provide a quantitative theory of the hot wind component in weak-wind O dwarfs that answers the following:

1. Identify the stellar/wind parameters (e.g. effective temperature, luminosity, surface gravity, metallicity, magnetic field, rotation, clumping structure) that determine whether forbidden high-ionization fine-structure mid-IR emission lines are produced, and explain in these terms why 10 Lac and μ Col require different wind diagnostics.

2. Determine whether, in a given weak-wind star, the hot phase represents only the high-temperature tail of a continuous wind-structure (temperature/density) distribution, or whether it can constitute the dominant component of the wind mass flux.

3. Characterize the transition between these two regimes as a function of the controlling parameters: is it smooth (continuous) or does it occur abruptly at some threshold, and locate any such threshold in parameter space.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns an actively discussed open issue in massive-star wind research. Recent JWST mid-IR observations (e.g. Law et al. 2024 on 10 Lac) provide new but partial empirical input, and no theoretical or observational consensus has been established on how regime-dependent the hot wind phase is or whether the transition to a dominant hot component in weak-wind stars is smooth. The status appears open.
